
## Demand Prediction
This chapter turns to the underlying question our business client asks: are machine learning models worth their keep in predicting ride-hailing demand. We approach it the way a fleet operator would, weighing predictive gains against the practical cost of adopting more complex methods.

Two questions organize the analysis. First, can support vector machines and neural networks predict demand reliably, and do they improve compared to simple historical averages by enough to justify the effort of building, tuning, and maintaining them?

Second, how should the data be represented? We compare uniform hexagonal grid cells against administrative community areas, and hourly demand slices against coarser time buckets, to determine which spatial and temporal resolution best supports accurate prediction.

To assess the following models in a comparable way, we carry two measures through the chapter. MAE (mean absolute error) captures the average miss in trips for a given area and time, while $R^2$ measures how much of the genuine variation in demand a model reproduces (1.0 marking a perfect fit).


### Prediction using Support Vector Machines

We modeled Chicago taxi demand using Support Vector Machines (SVM) at an H3 hexagon (resolution 6) 1-hour spatio-temporal
resolution to optimize high-frequency fleet dispatch logistics.

To begin with, we had to select suitable features and preprocess the data. To prevent critical data leakage and establish
strict structural boundaries, we excluded nine variables that are only known after a
trip concludes, such as the number of active vehicles, the average idle times of vehicles, the average trip duration.
Next, to avoid temporal leakage, the dataset of ~289,000 entries was partitioned using a strict chronological split (80% train / 20% test), reserving the final ~58,000 intervals for validation. Finally, the location identifiers (community areas and H3 hexagons) are one-hot encoded, allowing the model to learn a separate intercept for each neighborhood.

To establish an initial understanding of feature importances, we conducted a linear coefficients analysis. This revealed
that Point of Interest (POI) data strongly drives trip demand, led by density metrics such as number of hotels per squared
km and number of attractions per km2. Conversely, local weather metrics like the apparent temperature and amount of rain
represent low-impact statistical noise.

As an initial benchmark, we evaluated a Linear Support Vector Regression model without a kernel. This baseline underperformed, yielding an
$R^2$ of 0.6134 ($\text{MAE} = 13.05$ trips). Its primary limitation was a severe boundary infraction: 34.52% of
predictions fell below zero, exposing the linear plane's inability to respect non-negative demand thresholds.

Subsequent grid-search optimization (detailed in @fig-grid-search) clearly identified the Radial Basis Function (RBF)
kernel as the most promising approach. It also revealed 1000 as most promosing value for the hyperparameter C.
However, exact RBF kernel training scales cubically ($O(N^3)$) with dataset size, rendering standard training
computationally intractable on our hardware. To bypass this bottleneck, we deployed a Nystroëm low-rank approximation
to project the infinite-dimensional RBF space onto a compact set of landmark points. We evaluated different landmark
counts alongside models with and without weather features, given that our previous linear coefficient analysis flagged
weather metrics as marginal. As shown in @fig-model-results, our top-performing configuration excluded weather data
entirely, climbing to 0.8734 $R^2$ and driving the MAE down to 6.49 trips.

While these performance metrics represent a robust fit, especially given a highly efficient training runtime of approximately 7.5 minutes, the model still produced negative predictions for 22.28% of intervals, which required clipping to zero. To naturally enforce physical boundary constraints, we developed a two-Stage Hurdle SVM Framework. Stage 1 (The Gatekeeper) utilizes an RBF-approximated LinearSVC binary classifier to map the active-demand perimeter ($1$ if active, $0$ if dead). Stage 2 (The Volume Engine) then runs an RBF-approximated
LinearSVR trained exclusively on active instances, shielding the regression plane from zero-floor distortions
(see @fig-hurdle-results for the exact results).

Despite a minor structural tendency to generate false zeros during low-demand hours, this optimized No Weather
Hurdle Model emerged as our champion architecture, achieving a 0.8751 $R^2$ and a 6.44 trips MAE.
Crucially, it maximizes variance capture while mathematically guaranteeing 0% negative boundary violations, rendering
it highly viable for production deployment.

We also explored how performance scales across different spatio-temporal resolutions. Decreasing temporal resolution
(aggregating from 1-hour to 6-hour and 24-hour windows) smooths high-frequency demand surges, naturally boosting variance
capture. The 6-Hour Hexagon (No Weather) model secured our highest raw fit at 0.9042 $R^2$ ($\text{MAE} = 32.66$ trips).
However, absolute errors scale with the larger temporal footprint, which limits its utility for real-time dispatching.

Shifting the spatial unit from uniform geometric hexagons to irregular, administrative boundaries (Census Tracts/Community
Areas) degrades true operational accuracy. The 24-Hour community area model yields a deceptively high 0.8929 $R^2$ but
suffers a massive absolute error distortion of 57.12 trips MAE (compared to the 24-Hour Hexagon's 26.98 MAE). This surge
in MAE is a textbook demonstration of the Modifiable Areal Unit Problem (MAUP). It is driven primarily by the Scale Effect:
because administrative Community Areas are larger on average (~7.68 $km^2$) than Resolution 7 hexagons (~5.16 $km^2$), they
aggregate a much higher absolute volume of hourly trips, naturally inflating scale-dependent absolute metrics like MAE.
Furthermore, the Zone Effect introduces irregular boundaries and mismatched spatial centroids, warping the distance metrics
calculated on the SVM hyperplane. A full comparison of models can be found in @fig-model-comparison-r-squared and
@fig-model-comparison-mae.
